methods.label: Check every possible length
methods.explanation:
Six consecutive positive integers have sum at least
\[
1+2+3+4+5+6=21>15.
\]
Any longer run has an even larger minimum sum. Therefore only lengths \(2,3,4,5\) need checking.

Let \(a\) be the smallest integer in a run. The remaining integers are \(a+1,a+2,\ldots\), so the four possible lengths give
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\text{ terms: }&2a+1=15 &&\Rightarrow a=7,\\
3\text{ terms: }&3a+3=15 &&\Rightarrow a=4,\\
4\text{ terms: }&4a+6=15 &&\Rightarrow a=\frac94,\\
5\text{ terms: }&5a+10=15 &&\Rightarrow a=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The four-term case is invalid because its starting value is not an integer. The other cases give
\[
\{7,8\},\qquad \{4,5,6\},\qquad \{1,2,3,4,5\}.
\]
Every possible length has been checked, and each length and starting value determine exactly one set. Thus no valid set is omitted or counted twice. There are \(\boxed{3}\) sets, choice C.
methods.levelReason: A small finite bound and four simple linear equations suffice; no general sequence formula or number-theory theorem is needed.
